children.text:
The development of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates through
hole-doping relies on the controlled synthesis of Ni in a high oxidation
state, followed by topotactic reduction to a very low oxidation state. So
far, superconductivity has been realized only in epitaxial thin films. Here
we integrate these techniques with heterostructures that include an
epitaxial soluble buffer layer, enabling the release of freestanding (Nd,Sr)

structural and electronic properties to those of optimized thin films,
with lateral dimensions ranging from millimetres to ~100 μm, depending
on the degree of strain released with respect to the initial substrate. The
changes in the superconducting transition temperature upon release
of the heterostructure mirror those reported for variations in substrate
and pressure, suggesting a common underlying response to strain in the
infinite-layer nickelate superconductivity. These freestanding structures
will facilitate a range of experimental studies without the constraints
ofsubstrates.
In recent years, the application of soft chemistry techniques to oxide
thinfilmsandheterostructureshasopenedpathwaysforsynthesizing
metastable materials and establishing unique sample geometries.
Thediscoveryofsuperconductivityinhole-dopedinfinite-layernick-

of oxygen from a parent perovskite phase. This process was initially
demonstrated in bulk powders2,3 and subsequently in epitaxial thin
films4,5,wherethesubstratewasessentialtostabilizingtheinfinite-layer
structure with uniform crystalline orientation. Another important
example has been the creation of freestanding single-crystal oxide
films and heterostructures, either by dissolving the substrate itself6,7
or by embedding a sacrificial layer in a heterostructure8,9.

istry techniques to create superconducting freestanding nickelate

One approach would be to first lift off the perovskite nickelate
heterostructure and then perform topotactic reduction, given that
the infinite-layer nickelate phase is susceptible to re-oxidation and
degradation from ambient oxygen and water19,20. In addition, the
direct synthesis of released perovskite nickelate heterostructures
enablesustofocusonlattice-matchingoftheperovskitealone,which
has been shown to considerably impact the overall crystallinity15.
However,wefoundthat,despitetheabilitytosynthesizehigh-quality
doped freestanding Nd0.85Sr0.15NiO3, the subsequent topochemical
reduction resulted in insulating transport properties and very low
crystallinity (Supplementary Fig. 1). Although this result may not
be definitive, we directed our efforts to first create the infinite-layer
phase before release.
Several considerations must be taken into account for this
approach.First,thecriterionofminimizingepitaxialmismatchneeds
tobecentredontheinfinite-layerNd1−xSrxNiO2,whichiswell-matched
bytheSrTiO3 (STO)substrateandSr2Ca1Al2O6 (SCAO)sacrificiallayer21,
so that the heterostructure liftoff proceeds with a modest release of
~0.5% compressive strain3. However, the initially grown Nd1−xSrxNiO3
has a large epitaxial mismatch of ~2.6% tensile strain22. As a point of
comparison, we also studied freestanding heterostructures synthe-
sized on NdGaO3 (NGO) substrates using a Sr0.5Ca2.5Al2O6 sacrificial
layer21, which better matches the perovskite Nd1−xSrxNiO3 but results
in higher (~1.6%) compressive strain3 with respect to Nd1−xSrxNiO2.
Another consideration is to minimize the risk of degradation of the
infinite-layernickelatephaseduringheterostructurerelease,whenthe
filmisexposedtowater,oxygenandmildheating.Toaddressthis,STO
capping layers (8–20 unit cells (u.c.)) were grown epitaxially on both
sides of the nickelate layer to encapsulate and protect the nickelate
fromtheenvironment23.

Figure 3a–d presents high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) scan-
ning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images of an STO/
Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2/STO heterostructure transferred onto a silicon nitride
(SiNx) TEM window. Compared to previous studies of Nd1 − xSrxNiO2
thin films grown on STO substrates19,25, the cross-sectional STEM
image in Fig. 3a shows a highly crystalline structure with a surpris-
inglylowdensityofextendeddefects,consistentwithwhatisinferred
from the XRD characterization presented above. The ADF image and
elemental electron energy loss spectroscopy mapping in Fig. 3d
show sharp interfaces with limited signs of interdiffusion beyond the
single-unit-cellreconstruction28,29 acrossthetwointerfacesofSTOand
Nd0.80Sr0.20NiO2.Crucially,theoverallhomogeneityoftheSTEMimage,
alongwiththemacroscopicuniformityobservedintheopticalmicro-
scopeimage(Fig.1h),indicatestherobustnessoftheheterostructure,
particularly the nickelate layer, after release from the substrate. The
freestandinggeometryitselfprovidesanattractiveanddirectsample
for plan-view imaging, as shown in the HAADF STEM image in Fig. 3b.
Together with the strain mapping shown in Fig. 3c highlighting the
Ruddlesden–Popper faults (Methods), the overall structure of the
extended defects can be visualized and shows that the domains of
faults are sparse and isolated from each other.

substrate.
Theseobservationsmotivatedustocompareourcurrentresults
with previous reports on (Pr or Nd)1−xSrxNiO2 thin films (Fig. 5), focus-
ing on the possible correlation of Tc and strain, previously mediated
by varying the substrate-induced epitaxial strain14,15 and by pressure
appliedtothin-filmsamples16.(Notethatforthehigh-pressureresults16,
thenickelatein-planelatticeconstantsareassumedtofollowthoseof
theSTOsubstrate,compressingunderisotropicpressureviathebulk
STOresponse31,andSupplementaryFig.10presentstheTc dependence
on the cell volume.) It should again be emphasized that the degree
of disorder probably varies across the samples in this comparison,
as discussed above, as well as the specific hole-doping values (here
chosen in the vicinity of optimal doping). Despite these caveats, a
rather uniform rate of increase in Tc is found with decreasing in-plane
lattice constant, indicating that Tc is increasing with larger electronic
bandwidth. The microscopic origin of this trend, and the ultimate
limit on superconductivity that is implied, is an important question
forfurtherinvestigation.

Topochemical reduction
Theas-grownheterostructureswerelooselywrappedwithaluminium
foil and inserted into a Pyrex glass tube along with ~0.15 g of calcium
hydride (97% purity, Sigma-Aldrich). The tubes were pumped with a
rotary vane pump for 10 min to reach a pressure below 5 mtorr, and
then sealed with a hydrogen torch. The sealed glass tubes were sub-
sequentlyputinatubefurnaceandrampedto330–360 °Catarateof
10 °C min−1, annealed for 2–6 h, and cooled to room temperature at a
rateof~2 °C min−1.

children.text:
Heterostructure liftoff and transfer
Thereducedheterostructurefilmswerespin-coatedwithA8950poly-
methyl methacrylate (PMMA) at a speed of 3,500 r.p.m. for 60 s with
a ramping rate of 1,000 r.p.m. s−1 (thickness ~1 μm) and then cured
at 135 °C for 7.5 min. Sample edges were exposed by scratching with
a tungsten pen, where water could enter and start etching the sacri-
ficial layer. Sheets of plasma-treated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)
(~2 × 2 mm2) were then applied as a mechanical support. The samples
were put in deionized water until the sacrificial layers had been fully
dissolved. The released heterostructures were scooped out of the
water with a 3-mm-radius metal ring and transferred onto a target
substrate, such as a Si/SiO2 wafer or a SiNx membrane, with circular
holes 2 μm in diameter (Norcada). The samples were then dried at
60 °C for 5 min and subsequently 110 °C for 10 min. After heating, the
samplesweredippedintoacetoneatroomtemperaturetodissolvethe
PMMA(~10 min),untilthePDMShadnaturallybeenreleasedfromthe
samples. Finally, the samples were dipped in isopropanol for 5 min to
removeall other residues.
